In an experiment four quantities $a, b, c$ and $d$ are measured with percentage error $1 \%, 2 \%, 3 \%$ and $4 \%$ respectively. Quantity $P$ is calculated as follows
$P=\frac{a^3 b^2}{c d} \%$, Error in $P$ is
questions.solution:
Here, $P=\frac{a^3 b^2}{c d} \begin{aligned}
\therefore \frac{\Delta P}{P} & \times 100 = \left(\frac{3 \Delta a}{a}+\frac{2 \Delta b}{b}+\frac{\Delta c}{c}+\frac{\Delta d^{\prime}}{d}\right) \times 100 \\
= & 3 \frac{\Delta a}{a} \times 100+2 \frac{\Delta b}{b} \times 100+\frac{\Delta c}{c} \times 100+\frac{\Delta d^{\prime}}{d} \times 100 \\
= & 3 \times 1+2 \times 2+3+4 \\
= & 3+4+3+4=14 \%
\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
Finding the angle between the vectors:
$\begin{aligned}
& |\mathrm{A} \times \mathrm{B}|=\sqrt{3}(\mathrm{AB}) \\
& |\mathrm{A}||\mathrm{B}| \sin (\theta)=\sqrt{3}|\mathrm{~A}||\mathrm{B}| \cos (\theta)
\end{aligned}\)
Cancelling both sides we get
$\begin{aligned}
& $\sin$(\theta)=\sqrt{3} $\cos$(\theta) \\
& $\frac{$\sin$(\theta)}{$\cos$(\theta)}=$\sqrt{3} \\
& $\tan$(\theta)=\sqrt{3}
\end{aligned}\)
Hence \(\theta=60^{\circ}\)
Hence the angle between A and B is \(60^{\circ}\)

questions.q: If $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=2 \hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{r}=3 \hat{i}+2 \hat{j}-2 \hat{k}$, then the scalar and vector products of $\vec{F}$ and $\vec{r}$ have the magnitudes respectively as:
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& \overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=2 \hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k} \\
& \vec{r}=3 \hat{i}+2 \hat{j}-2 \hat{k}  \text{ (given) }
\end{aligned}$
The scalar product of $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}} and \vec{r}$ is
$\begin{aligned}
\vec{F} . \vec{r} & =(2)(3)+(1)(2)+(-1)(-2) \\
& =6+2+2=10
\end{aligned}$
The vector product of $\vec{F} and \vec{r}$ is
$\begin{aligned}
\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}} \times \vec{r} & =\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\
2 & 1 & -1 \\
3 & 2 & -2
\end{array}\right| \\
& =\hat{i}[(1 \times-2)-(2 \times-1)]-\hat{j}[(2 \times-2) \\
& -(-1 \times 3)]+\hat{k}[(2 \times 2)-(3 \times 1)] \\
& =\hat{i}(0)-\hat{j}(-1)+\hat{k}(1)=\hat{j}+\hat{k}
\end{aligned}$
Magnitude $= \sqrt{(1)^2+(1)^2}=\sqrt{2}$

questions.q:
Read the following statements carefully:

Statement I: The integer used to divide the sum of measurements when calculating an average is an exact number with infinite significant figures.
Statement II: If a raw calculated mean is $3.455 \text{ cm}$, it is rounded to $3.46 \text{ cm}$ to retain 3 significant figures.
Statement III: The sum of $1.2 \text{ cm}$ and $3.45 \text{ cm}$ has three significant figures.
Statement IV: When averaging measurements of the same precision, the final result retains the same number of decimal places as the original measurements.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Statement I is correct: The count of measurements is an exact number and has infinite significant figures.

Statement II is correct: To retain 3 significant figures in $3.455 \text{ cm}$, the digit to be dropped is 5. Since the preceding digit (5) is odd, it is increased by 1, giving $3.46 \text{ cm}$.

Statement III is incorrect: According to the rules of significant figures for addition, the result must have the same number of decimal places as the term with the least number of decimal places. $1.2 \text{ cm} + 3.45 \text{ cm} = 4.65 \text{ cm}$. This must be rounded to one decimal place. Since the digit to be dropped is 5 and the preceding digit (6) is even, it is left unchanged. The result is $4.6 \text{ cm}$, which has two significant figures, not three.

Statement IV is correct: Since the sum of the measurements retains the same number of decimal places as the original data, and division by an exact integer does not alter this precision, the final average retains the same number of decimal places.

Therefore, exactly three statements (I, II, and IV) are correct.

Answer: Only three

questions.q: The heat dissipated in a resistor is given by the formula $H = I^2 R t$. In a laboratory experiment, the measured values of current ($I$), resistance ($R$), and time ($t$) are recorded as $I = (10 \pm 0.2)\text{ A}$, $R = (5 \pm 0.1)\ \Omega$, and $t = (100 \pm 1)\text{ s}$. The maximum percentage error in the calculated value of heat dissipated $H$ will be:
questions.solution:
Percentage error in current $I = \dfrac{0.2}{10} \times 100 = 2\%$

Percentage error in resistance $R = \dfrac{0.1}{5} \times 100 = 2\%$

Percentage error in time $t = \dfrac{1}{100} \times 100 = 1\%$

The formula for heat dissipated is $H = I^2 R t$.

The maximum percentage error in $H$ is given by:
$\dfrac{\Delta H}{H} \times 100 = 2\left(\dfrac{\Delta I}{I} \times 100\right) + \dfrac{\Delta R}{R} \times 100 + \dfrac{\Delta t}{t} \times 100$

$\dfrac{\Delta H}{H} \times 100 = 2(2\%) + 2\% + 1\% = 4\% + 2\% + 1\% = 7\%$

Answer: $7\%$

questions.q: A student measures human body temperature by placing a thermometer under the armpit. This method always gives a temperature reading that is lower than the actual internal body temperature. According to the classification of errors in measurement, this specific type of error is an example of:
questions.solution:
According to NCERT, measuring temperature under the armpit will always give a reading lower than the actual body temperature. This is a consistent error occurring in one direction due to a flawed procedure, which falls under the category of systematic errors, specifically termed as 'imperfection in experimental technique or procedure'.

It is not an instrumental error because the thermometer itself may be perfectly calibrated. It is not a personal error because it is not caused by individual carelessness or parallax. It is not a random error because the reading does not fluctuate unpredictably but is consistently lower.

Answer: Imperfection in experimental technique

(C) Fractional error(III) $0.06$
(D) Percentage error(IV) $6\%$

questions.solution:
First, calculate the true value (mean of the observations):
$T_m = \dfrac{2.3 + 2.4 + 2.6 + 2.7}{4} = \dfrac{10.0}{4} = 2.5\text{ s}$.

$\Delta T_3 = |2.6 - 2.5| = 0.1\text{ s}$

$\Delta T_m = \dfrac{0.2 + 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.2}{4} = \dfrac{0.6}{4} = 0.15\text{ s}$.
So, (B) matches with (II).

Calculate the fractional error:
$\text{Fractional error} = \dfrac{\Delta T_m}{T_m} = \dfrac{0.15}{2.5} = 0.06$.
So, (C) matches with (III).

Calculate the percentage error:
$\text{Percentage error} = \text{Fractional error} \times 100 = 0.06 \times 100 = 6\%$.
So, (D) matches with (IV).

questions.q: A student measures the mass and radius of a solid sphere to calculate its density. If the percentage errors in the measurement of mass and radius are $2\%$ and $1.5\%$ respectively, the maximum percentage error in the calculated density of the sphere will be
questions.solution:
The density of a sphere is given by the formula:

$\rho = \dfrac{M}{V} = \dfrac{M}{\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3}$

The maximum percentage error in density is given by the sum of the percentage errors of the individual quantities multiplied by their respective powers. Constants like $\dfrac{4}{3}\pi$ do not contribute to the error.

$\dfrac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} \times 100 = \left(\dfrac{\Delta M}{M} \times 100\right) + 3\left(\dfrac{\Delta R}{R} \times 100\right)$

Given that the percentage error in mass is $2\%$ and in radius is $1.5\%$:

$\dfrac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} \times 100 = 2\% + 3(1.5\%)$

$\dfrac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} \times 100 = 2\% + 4.5\% = 6.5\%$

Thus, the maximum percentage error in the calculated density is $6.5\%$.

Answer: $6.5\%$

First, find the fourth reading.
The mean of $4$ readings is $2.00\text{ s}$, so their sum is $4 \times 2.00 = 8.00\text{ s}$.
The sum of the three given readings is $1.98 + 1.99 + 2.02 = 5.99\text{ s}$.
Therefore, the fourth reading is $8.00 - 5.99 = 2.01\text{ s}$.

$\Delta T_2 = |1.99 - 2.00| = 0.01\text{ s}$
$\Delta T_3 = |2.02 - 2.00| = 0.02\text{ s}$
$\Delta T_4 = |2.01 - 2.00| = 0.01\text{ s}$

Now, find the mean absolute error:
$\Delta T_m = \dfrac{0.02 + 0.01 + 0.02 + 0.01}{4} = \dfrac{0.06}{4} = 0.015\text{ s}$

Finally, calculate the percentage relative error:
$\%\text{ error} = \left(\dfrac{\Delta T_m}{T_m}\right) \times 100$
$\%\text{ error} = \left(\dfrac{0.015}{2.00}\right) \times 100 = 0.75\%$

Answer: $0.75\%$

questions.q: In an experiment to determine the specific resistance ($\rho$) of a wire, the formula used is $\rho = \dfrac{R \pi d^2}{4l}$, where $R$ is the resistance, $d$ is the diameter, and $l$ is the length of the wire. If the maximum permissible percentage error in the determination of $\rho$ is $8\%$, and the measured percentage errors in $R$ and $l$ are $2\%$ and $1\%$ respectively, what is the maximum permissible percentage error in the measurement of the diameter ($d$)?
questions.solution:
The formula for specific resistance is $\rho = \dfrac{R \pi d^2}{4l}$.

The maximum percentage error in $\rho$ is given by the sum of the percentage errors of the individual quantities, taking into account their powers. Errors always add up to give the maximum possible error, regardless of whether the quantity is in the numerator or denominator:

$\dfrac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} \times 100 = \dfrac{\Delta R}{R} \times 100 + 2 \left( \dfrac{\Delta d}{d} \times 100 \right) + \dfrac{\Delta l}{l} \times 100$

Given that the maximum percentage error in $\rho$ is $8\%$, in $R$ is $2\%$, and in $l$ is $1\%$, we can substitute these values into the equation:

$8\% = 2\% + 2 \times (\text{percentage error in } d) + 1\%$

$8\% = 3\% + 2 \times (\text{percentage error in } d)$

$2 \times (\text{percentage error in } d) = 5\%$

$\text{Percentage error in } d = 2.5\%$

Answer: $2.5\%$

The maximum percentage error in $\rho$ is given by the sum of the percentage errors of the individual quantities, taking into account their powers. Errors always add up to give the maximum possible error, regardless of whether the quantity is in the numerator or denominator:

$\dfrac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} \times 100 = \dfrac{\Delta R}{R} \times 100 + 2 \left( \dfrac{\Delta d}{d} \times 100 \right) + \dfrac{\Delta l}{l} \times 100$

Given that the maximum percentage error in $\rho$ is $8\%$, in $R$ is $2\%$, and in $l$ is $1\%$, we can substitute these values into the equation:

$8\% = 3\% + 2 \times (\text{percentage error in } d)$

$2 \times (\text{percentage error in } d) = 5\%$

The maximum percentage error in $g$ is the sum of the percentage errors in the measured quantities, multiplied by the absolute values of their respective powers. Constants like $4\pi^2$ do not contribute to the error.

$\dfrac{\Delta T}{T} \times 100 = \dfrac{4\%}{2} = 2\%$

The percentage error in the measurement of time period $T$ is $2\%$.

questions.q: A student measures the time of flight of a projectile five times and records the following readings: $4.6\text{ s}$, $4.8\text{ s}$, $5.0\text{ s}$, $5.2\text{ s}$, and $5.4\text{ s}$. Which of the following statements regarding this set of measurements is incorrect?
options: The most probable true value of the time of flight is $5.0\text{ s}$.
The mean absolute error is zero because positive and negative deviations cancel each other out.
The fractional error in the measurement is $0.048$.
The absolute error in the first reading is $0.4\text{ s}$.
questions.solution:
First, calculate the mean value of the observations, which represents the most probable true value:
$t_{mean} = \dfrac{4.6 + 4.8 + 5.0 + 5.2 + 5.4}{5} = \dfrac{25.0}{5} = 5.0\text{ s}$.

Next, find the absolute errors in each measurement by taking the magnitude of the difference between each reading and the mean value:

$\Delta t_2 = |4.8 - 5.0| = 0.2\text{ s}$
$\Delta t_3 = |5.0 - 5.0| = 0.0\text{ s}$
$\Delta t_4 = |5.2 - 5.0| = 0.2\text{ s}$
$\Delta t_5 = |5.4 - 5.0| = 0.4\text{ s}$

The mean absolute error is the arithmetic mean of these absolute errors:
$\Delta t_{mean} = \dfrac{0.4 + 0.2 + 0.0 + 0.2 + 0.4}{5} = \dfrac{1.2}{5} = 0.24\text{ s}$.
Absolute errors are magnitudes and are always positive, so they do not algebraically cancel out. Thus, the statement claiming the mean absolute error is zero is incorrect.

The fractional error is given by:
$\text{Fractional error} = \dfrac{\Delta t_{mean}}{t_{mean}} = \dfrac{0.24}{5.0} = 0.048$.

Answer: The mean absolute error is zero because positive and negative deviations cancel each other out.

questions.q: Four measurements of the mass of a block are recorded as $2.01 \mathrm{~g}$, $2.02 \mathrm{~g}$, $2.03 \mathrm{~g}$, and $2.05 \mathrm{~g}$. The final reported mass of the block, expressed in the standard form (mean $\pm$ mean absolute error) with appropriate significant figures, is:
questions.solution:
First, calculate the mean of the mass measurements:
Sum $= 2.01 + 2.02 + 2.03 + 2.05 = 8.11 \mathrm{~g}$
Mean $= \dfrac{8.11}{4} = 2.0275 \mathrm{~g}$

Since the original measurements have two decimal places, the mean must be rounded to two decimal places. Rounding $2.0275 \mathrm{~g}$ gives $2.03 \mathrm{~g}$.

Next, calculate the absolute errors for each measurement using the rounded mean ($2.03 \mathrm{~g}$):
$|2.01 - 2.03| = 0.02 \mathrm{~g}$
$|2.02 - 2.03| = 0.01 \mathrm{~g}$
$|2.03 - 2.03| = 0.00 \mathrm{~g}$
$|2.05 - 2.03| = 0.02 \mathrm{~g}$

Sum of absolute errors $= 0.02 + 0.01 + 0.00 + 0.02 = 0.05 \mathrm{~g}$
Mean absolute error $= \dfrac{0.05}{4} = 0.0125 \mathrm{~g}$

The mean absolute error must also be rounded to two decimal places to match the precision of the mean. Rounding $0.0125 \mathrm{~g}$ to two decimal places gives $0.01 \mathrm{~g}$.

The final reported result is $2.03 \pm 0.01 \mathrm{~g}$.

Answer: $2.03 \pm 0.01 \mathrm{~g}$

Substituting the values:
$\dfrac{\Delta K}{K} \times 100 = 5\% + 2(4\%) = 5\% + 8\% = 13\%$

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The random error in a measurement can be minimized by taking a large number of observations and finding their arithmetic mean.
Reason (R): Random errors occur irregularly and are equally likely to be positive or negative.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
Random errors are those errors which occur irregularly and hence are random with respect to sign and size. They can be positive or negative. When a large number of observations are taken, the positive and negative random errors tend to cancel each other out. Therefore, the arithmetic mean of all observations is taken as the most accurate reading, which effectively minimizes the random error. Thus, both Assertion and Reason are correct, and the Reason correctly explains why taking the mean minimizes the error.

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

questions.q: A student measures the time taken for a stone to fall from a cliff. The recorded readings are $9.8\text{ s}$, $9.9\text{ s}$, $10.1\text{ s}$, and $10.2\text{ s}$. The student uses the formula $h = \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$ to calculate the height of the cliff. Assuming the acceleration due to gravity $g$ is known exactly, what is the percentage error in the calculated height?
questions.solution:
First, find the mean value of the time measurements:
$t_{mean} = \dfrac{9.8 + 9.9 + 10.1 + 10.2}{4} = \dfrac{40.0}{4} = 10.0\text{ s}$.

Next, calculate the absolute errors for each reading:
$\Delta t_1 = |9.8 - 10.0| = 0.2\text{ s}$
$\Delta t_2 = |9.9 - 10.0| = 0.1\text{ s}$
$\Delta t_3 = |10.1 - 10.0| = 0.1\text{ s}$
$\Delta t_4 = |10.2 - 10.0| = 0.2\text{ s}$

The mean absolute error in time is:
$\Delta t_{mean} = \dfrac{0.2 + 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.2}{4} = \dfrac{0.6}{4} = 0.15\text{ s}$.

The percentage error in the time measurement is:
$\dfrac{\Delta t_{mean}}{t_{mean}} \times 100 = \dfrac{0.15}{10.0} \times 100 = 1.5\%$.

The height is calculated using $h = \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$. Since $g$ and $\dfrac{1}{2}$ are exact constants, the relative error in $h$ depends only on $t$. According to the rule for propagation of errors for a quantity raised to a power:
$\dfrac{\Delta h}{h} \times 100 = 2 \times \left(\dfrac{\Delta t}{t} \times 100\right)$

Percentage error in $h = 2 \times 1.5\% = 3.0\%$.

Answer: $3.0\%$

questions.q: The heat dissipated in a resistance wire is given by Joule's law of heating, $H = I^2 R t$. In an experiment, the maximum percentage errors in the measurement of heat dissipated ($H$), resistance ($R$), and time ($t$) are $9\%$, $2\%$, and $1\%$ respectively. The percentage error in the measurement of current ($I$) is:
questions.solution:
The formula for heat dissipated is $H = I^2 R t$.

The maximum percentage error in $H$ is given by the sum of the percentage errors of its factors, multiplied by their respective powers:
$\dfrac{\Delta H}{H} \times 100 = 2 \left( \dfrac{\Delta I}{I} \times 100 \right) + \left( \dfrac{\Delta R}{R} \times 100 \right) + \left( \dfrac{\Delta t}{t} \times 100 \right)$

Given the percentage errors:
$\dfrac{\Delta H}{H} \times 100 = 9\%$
$\dfrac{\Delta R}{R} \times 100 = 2\%$
$\dfrac{\Delta t}{t} \times 100 = 1\%$

Substitute these values into the error equation:
$9\% = 2 \left( \dfrac{\Delta I}{I} \times 100 \right) + 2\% + 1\%$

$9\% = 2 \left( \dfrac{\Delta I}{I} \times 100 \right) + 3\%$

$2 \left( \dfrac{\Delta I}{I} \times 100 \right) = 9\% - 3\% = 6\%$

$\dfrac{\Delta I}{I} \times 100 = \dfrac{6\%}{2} = 3\%$

The percentage error in the measurement of current is $3\%$.

Answer: $3\%$

questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding errors in measurement is incorrect?
options: Systematic errors tend to be in one direction, either positive or negative.
Systematic errors can be estimated and the necessary corrections can be applied to the readings.
Random errors occur irregularly and are unpredictable with respect to sign and size.
Imperfection in experimental procedure or technique always leads to a random error.
questions.solution:
Systematic errors are those that tend to be in one direction, either positive or negative. Because their causes are known, they can often be estimated and necessary corrections can be applied to the readings.

Random errors occur irregularly and are unpredictable with respect to sign and size.

Imperfection in experimental procedure or technique (such as ignoring the buoyancy of air or measuring temperature under the armpit) is a known, consistent flaw that biases the result in a specific direction. Therefore, it is a source of systematic error, not a random error. The statement claiming it leads to a random error is incorrect.

Answer: Imperfection in experimental procedure or technique always leads to a random error.

or $\quad \frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho}=0.0153+0.1+0.02$

$13.5 \% \approx 13 \%$.

questions.q: If $\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{C}$ and that $\mathbf{C}$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf{A}$. What is the angle between $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, if $|\mathbf{A}|=|\mathbf{C}|$ ?
questions.solution:
Given, $A+B=C$
and $\mathrm{B}=\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{A}$
Since, $\mathbf{C} \perp \mathbf{A}$, therefore
$B^2=C^2+A^2$
Also, $|\mathbf{C}|=|\mathbf{A}|$, therefore
$B^2=2 A^2 \Rightarrow B=\sqrt{2} A$
Now, $A^2+B^2+2 A B \cos \theta=C^2=A^2$
$\therefore \quad \cos \theta=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
This gives $\quad \theta=\frac{3 \pi}{4} \mathrm{rad}$
